hints: Start at the left of Fig. 8.1 and follow the impulse direction - from receptor cells toward the spinal cord. Which end must receive information first?
Remember a sensory neurone has its cell body off to one side. The fibre before the cell body and the fibre after it have different names.
The fine branching fibres touching the receptor cells are for collection, while the long myelinated fibre labelled B carries that depolarisation toward the cell body.
The round structure containing the nucleus is the cell body, and the long myelinated fibre leaving it toward the CNS terminals is the axon.
walkthrough:
Picture the job of a sensory neurone**
Think of a sensory neurone as a one-way wire from a receptor to the CNS. On the left you have receptor cells, in the middle a cell body pushed to the side, and on the right branched endings that will synapse in the CNS. Impulses always travel receptor -> dendrites -> dendron -> cell body -> axon -> terminals.

Sort A and B at the receptor end**
A points to the tiny branched fibres actually contacting the receptor cells. Those are dendrites - they pick up the receptor potential. All those dendrites join into the long myelinated fibre B that runs to the cell body. In a sensory neurone this first long fibre is called the dendron, though it behaves like an axon for conduction.

Sort C and D after the cell body**
C brackets the swollen part containing the nucleus and most cytoplasm. That is the cell body, or soma. D brackets the second long myelinated fibre running from the cell body to the branched terminals on the right. That is the axon of the sensory neurone.
Final answer: A - dendrite(s); B - dendron / sensory axon; C - cell body of neurone / soma; D - axon.

hints: Think about what myelin is made of - fatty Schwann cell membranes wrapped many times. What does fat do to the movement of ions and charge leakage?
If charge cannot leak out and depolarisation cannot happen under the wrapping, where along the axon can new action potentials be regenerated?
walkthrough:
Why insulation matters**
Myelin is many layers of Schwann cell membrane, mostly lipid. It acts as an electrical insulator, preventing $Na^+$ and $K^+$ movement across the axon membrane underneath. That means no influx of $Na^+$ and no regeneration of an action potential in myelinated regions.

How jumping speeds things up**
Voltage-gated channels are concentrated at the gaps called nodes of Ranvier. Depolarisation at one node sets up a local circuit to the next node, where a fresh action potential is triggered. The impulse effectively jumps from node to node - saltatory conduction - so it travels much faster than the wave of depolarisation in an unmyelinated fibre.

Final answer: Myelin insulates the axon so depolarisation / action potentials occur only at nodes of Ranvier; local circuits form between nodes so the impulse jumps node to node by saltatory conduction, which is faster.

hints: Compare Fig. 8.3 bars left to right with Fig. 8.2 traces left to right. What happens with the smallest stimulus that only reaches about $-55$ $mV$ compared to the larger ones that reach $-50$ $mV$?
For the three larger stimuli, look carefully at the height of the spikes near $+40$ $mV$. Does a taller stimulus bar give a taller spike?
walkthrough:
Separate sub-threshold from supra-threshold**
In Fig. 8.2 the resting potential is about $-70$ $mV$ and the dashed line marks about $-50$ $mV$ threshold. The first small stimulus in Fig. 8.3 produces only a small receptor potential to about $-55$ $mV$ that falls back with no spike. The next three larger stimuli all push the membrane to threshold and each triggers a full spike to about $+40$ $mV$.

See the all-or-nothing rule**
Although stimulus strength in Fig. 8.3 keeps increasing from bar 2 to bar 4, the three action potentials in Fig. 8.2 are identical in amplitude. Once threshold is reached, the $Na^+$ channels open fully and the same sequence of depolarisation and repolarisation occurs. A stronger stimulus does not make a bigger action potential. That is the all-or-nothing law.

Final answer: Only a stimulus that depolarises the membrane to threshold (about $-50$ $mV$) triggers an action potential; all action potentials produced are the same size regardless of stimulus strength above threshold - the all-or-nothing response.
